title: Which side for the cord
translation: I once asked an expert on court customs: "A box has rings on the sides for the cord. Which side should the cord go on?"

He said, "There are two schools. One puts it on the left, at the end where a scroll has its roller, and the other on the right, where a scroll has its cover. So neither is wrong. Letter boxes mostly have it on the right. On a box for your personal things, the left is quite usual too."
original: 「{箱|はこ}のくりかたに{緒|を}を{著|つ}くる{事|こと}、いづ{方|かた}につけ{侍|はべ}るべきぞ。」と、ある{有職|いうそく}の{人|ひと}に{尋|たづ}ね{申|まう}し{侍|はべ}りしかば、
「{軸|ぢく}につけ{表紙|へうし}につくること、{両説|りやうせつ}なれば、{何|いづ}れも{難|なん}なし。
{文|ふみ}の{箱|はこ}は{多|おほ}くは{右|みぎ}につく。
{手箱|てばこ}には{軸|ぢく}につくるも{常|つね}のことなり。」と{仰|おほ}せられき。
literal: When I asked a certain person versed in court precedent, 'Attaching the cord to the kurikata of a box: on which side should one attach it?',
'Attaching it on the roller side or attaching it on the cover side: since there are two views, neither is at fault.
Letter boxes mostly attach it on the right.
For a hand box, attaching it on the roller side is also usual', he said.

notes.text: くりかた ({刳形|くりかた}): the fittings on the sides of a box, carved openings or metal rings, through which the cord ({緒|を}) runs to tie the lid down. The exact form varied, and commentators describe it in different ways.
{有職|いうそく}: an expert on court precedent and etiquette (compare sections 1 and 33).

notes.quote: 軸につけ表紙につくること
notes.text: The terms come from the handscroll. Unrolled from right to left, a scroll has its cover ({表紙|へうし}) at the right-hand end and its roller ({軸|ぢく}) at the left. Commentators take 'roller side' as the left side of the box and 'cover side' as the right, which fits the next sentence: letter boxes mostly on the right.

notes.quote: 両説なれば、何れも難なし
notes.text: {両説|りやうせつ}: 'two views', two accepted traditions. {難|なん}なし: 'no fault' (as in section 33, where the experts found {難|なん}なし in the new palace).
{手箱|てばこ}: a box for personal things kept close at hand, such as combs, make-up and small papers.
き: the past of things the writer experienced himself. Kenkō asked the question in person, and he reports the answer and nothing else.
